title: INTC Q3 deep dive: strong data center growth offsets PC challenges, outlook pressured by supply constraints
detail:
INTC Q3 deep dive: strong data center growth offsets PC challenges, outlook pressured by supply constraints
Kayode Omotosho
Sat, October 31, 2026 at 12:55 PM CDT 6 min read
INTC
Trade Intel on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Computer processor maker Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) reported Q3 2026 results topping the market's revenue expectations , with sales up 20.9% year on year to $16.51 billion. On the other hand, next quarter's revenue guidance of $15.5 billion was less impressive, coming in 8.9% below analysts' estimates. Its non-GAAP profit of $0.52 per share was 30.6% above analysts' consensus estimates.

Is now the time to buy INTC? Find out in our full research report (it's free).

Intel (INTC) Q3 2026 highlights:

Revenue $16.51 billion vs S&P analysts' estimates of $16.42 billion (20.9% year-on-year growth, 0.6% beat)

Adjusted EPS $0.52 vs S&P analysts' estimates of $0.40 (30.6% beat)

Adjusted operating income $3.23 billion vs analyst estimates of $2.65 billion (19.6% margin, 22% beat)

Revenue guidance $15.5 billion at the midpoint for Q4 2026, below analyst estimates of $17.02 billion

Adjusted EPS guidance $0.25 at the midpoint for Q4 2026, below analyst estimates of $0.44

Operating margin 15.3%, up from 5% in the same quarter last year

Inventory days outstanding 126, up from 118 in the previous quarter

Market capitalization $483.8 billion

StockStory's take

Intel's third quarter saw a sharp divergence between robust data center demand and ongoing weakness in the PC market, which contributed to a negative market reaction. Management attributed the upside in revenue to surging growth in its data center and AI segment, with CEO Lip-Bu Tan stating, "Demand for 2027 is significant, especially in CPU dense agentic rack scale infrastructure." However, persistent supply shortages and a challenging PC environment, including inventory corrections and memory cost pressures, held back broader performance.

Looking forward, Intel's guidance reflects ongoing caution, as supply limitations and external factors continue to weigh on visibility. Management acknowledged near-term headwinds, with CFO Dave Zinsner explaining, "The only little nuance is the first half of the year, we are still a bit constrained." While the company expects strong demand for server CPUs and new product launches such as Nova Lake, executives emphasized that memory shortages and a drawn-out inventory correction in the PC market will likely persist into the first half of next year.

Key insights from management's remarks

Management credited the quarter's performance to accelerating data center and AI momentum, but flagged persistent supply and memory headwinds limiting output and PC demand.

Data center and AI momentum: Intel's data center and AI segment (DCAI) experienced its strongest revenue growth in 15 years, driven by demand for its Granite Rapids and Clearwater Forest server CPUs. This growth was attributed to increased hyperscale and enterprise customer adoption as AI workloads expand beyond traditional applications.

Advanced packaging and manufacturing constraints: Management highlighted industry-wide shortages of advanced organic substrates used in advanced packaging (EMIB) that are limiting output of high-demand server chips. Efforts to ramp capacity in Ireland, Oregon, and Arizona are underway, but supply tightness is expected to persist into next year.

Purpose-built silicon growth: The purpose-built silicon business, which includes customized chips for specific workloads, tripled over the past three years and is expected to triple again, reflecting demand from AI labs and new customer segments. This diversification is seen as vital to Intel's longer-term growth.

PC market correction: The client computing business (CCPG) faced an accelerated PC market downturn, with OEM partners aggressively reducing inventory due to rising memory prices and tight IT budgets. Management called the recent quarters "the most difficult" for PC demand in decades, with recovery dependent on improvements in memory availability and pricing.

Quantum computing acquisition: Intel announced its intent to acquire Classiq, an Israel-based quantum software provider, signaling a push to commercialize quantum computing and integrate it with its existing CPU, GPU, and ASIC platforms. Management sees this as a step toward becoming a "full stack revenue-generating quantum computing company."

title: Intel Has a Massive Warning for AMD Stock Investors. Is It Time to Book Profits Before Nov. 3?

Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) released its third-quarter results on Oct. 29, and shares of the company crashed more than 28% the following day.

The primary reason behind the bloodbath in Intel stock was its weaker-than-expected guidance. Though Intel guided for a strong year-over-year increase in both revenue and earnings, Wall Street was expecting more. However, the sharp drop in personal computer (PC) sales this year offset the impressive gains that Intel enjoyed in the data center segment.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

That doesn't bode well for Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD). Let's look at the reasons why.

Image source: Getty Images.

AMD's reliance on the PC market could dent investor confidence in the stock

When AMD released its second-quarter results in August, the company reported a healthy 23% year-over-year increase in revenue from sales of client central processing units (CPUs) for PCs. The segment's revenue landed at $3.1 billion, accounting for 27% of its top line.

Similarly, Intel's revenue from its client computing segment was up by 13% year over year in Q2 to $8.9 billion. However, the script flipped in Q3, with Intel reporting a 5% year-over-year drop in client computing revenue to $8.1 billion. The company blamed poor PC sales for this decline, which isn't surprising as the market has been going through a rough patch due to high memory costs and component shortages.

Counterpoint Research estimates that global PC shipments dropped 21% year over year in Q3. The firm expects Q4 to be even worse, with a 27% drop from the year-ago period. Similarly, Intel noted that the PC decline has accelerated recently amid high costs that are pressuring companies' IT budgets. So, AMD could feel the heat when it releases Q3 results after the market closes on Nov. 3.

Intel also pointed out that PC shipments will drop around 10% in 2027, with "year-over-year declines to be more pronounced during the first half." The situation could improve in the second half of 2027 due to easier comparisons from the year-ago period. However, AMD's client CPU business may face near-term challenges.

Should investors book profits in AMD ahead of its quarterly report?

AMD stock has jumped 90% over the past year, which is why investors may be wondering whether they should take profits off the table. Well, the broader market sentiment on artificial intelligence (AI) stocks suggests that booking profits could be the right move. However, if AMD suffers a steep fall following its Nov. 3 report, it may be a smart idea to buy it for multiple reasons.

According to a company press release, Intel reported third-quarter 2026 revenue of $16.51 billion, up 20.9% year on year, and non-GAAP earnings per share of $0.52. Both metrics cleared Wall Street's expectations, but the company's forward guidance disappointed investors. At the $15.5 billion midpoint, revenue guidance fell below analysts' expectations of $17.02 billion, while the adjusted profit forecast trailed consensus estimates of $0.44 per share.

Additionally, Chief Financial Officer David Zinsner indicated that personal computer market weakness was expected to continue through at least the first half of next year. The softer forecast and prolonged PC slump raised concerns over Intel's near-term profitability, triggering the sell-off.

Key Takeaways

Marvell Technology fell 14% in the past week on reported Lumentum talks, then in a chip selloff after Intel's weak outlook.

Lumentum's lasers would make Marvell a bigger Broadcom rival and give Coherent a competitor backed by Marvell's chips.

A deal would reportedly be paid in Marvell shares, so I'd wait for the share count.

Marvell Technology (MRVL:NASDAQ) stock is down 14% in the past week.

Bloomberg reported after Wednesday's close that Marvell is in advanced talks to buy Lumentum (LITE:NASDAQ), which would push it deeper into the AI networking Broadcom (AVGO:NASDAQ) sells and leave Coherent (COHR:NYSE) as the big laser maker not controlled by a chip designer. Then Intel (INTC:NASDAQ) gave a weak outlook after Thursday's close, sinking AI chip stocks again.

The Price Is in Shares

Lumentum was worth about $83 billion at the report, more than a third of Marvell's own value, while Marvell held just $3.93 billion in cash as of Aug. 1. So a deal would mean a lot of new shares, and investors balked. Analysts expect Marvell's normalized EPS to more than double, from $2.84 in the year ended January 2026 to $7.33 in the year ending January 2028:

MRVL Normalized EPS Estimates: 2024-2029 (TIKR)

The report shouldn't move those estimates yet. Paying in stock would add shares, but whether that lowers or raises EPS would depend on Lumentum's profits and the price Marvell pays. Marvell has paid in shares before: its share count jumped 19%, from 669 million in fiscal 2021 to 797 million in fiscal 2022, after it bought Inphi largely with stock:

MRVL Diluted Shares Outstanding: Fiscal 2021-2025 (TIKR)
Broadcom and Coherent Would Feel It

On a Bloomberg Intelligence podcast Thursday, analyst Mandeep Singh said small chipmakers like Marvell "don't have a choice but to go the acquisition route." Broadcom booked $16.7 billion of AI chip revenue in the quarter ended Aug. 2, and lasers would help Marvell chase it.

Coherent grew revenue 34% to $2.05 billion in the quarter ended June 30. Its early-November report should show whether customers wanting an independent laser supplier send it more orders.

Intel's Outlook Hit the Group

Intel guided fourth-quarter revenue to $15.0 billion to $16.0 billion, below expectations, and chip stocks fell with it on Friday, Marvell by another 10%. Amazon, one of Marvell's biggest custom-chip customers, reported the same evening, and its spending cuts the other way: its free cash flow was negative $42.4 billion over the trailing 12 months as it builds out AI.

title: Tom Lee Thinks One Investor Might Be Behind Nasdaq’s Stock Crash
detail:
Tom Lee Thinks One Investor Might Be Behind Nasdaq’s Stock Crash
Lockridge Okoth
Sat, October 31, 2026 at 8:31 AM CDT 2 min read
INTC
^IXIC
Trade Intel on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Tom Lee. Photo by BeInCrypto

Intel lost almost a third of its value on Friday. By the close, the Nasdaq Composite had sealed its worst month since March 2025, down 5.3%.

Tom Lee of Fundstrat, a Wall Street research firm, has another suspect. He thinks one big investor may have been forced to dump tech shares, leaving tech holders with the losses.

Why Tom Lee Thinks One Investor Was Forced to Sell

Speaking on CNBC as the Nasdaq slid on Friday, Lee said the market was fighting an "internal battle" and that the selling looked forced.

"Today looks like someone's getting liquidated. I don't know if it's an institution," he said.

By "liquidated," Lee means forced to sell. This happens when an investor buys shares with borrowed money and prices then fall. The lender wants its money back, so the investor has to sell at any price.

Selling that big drags prices even lower. Lee thinks that is what hit tech on Friday, not investors abandoning stocks.

As evidence, he pointed to a version of the S&P 500 that counts every company equally, so a small firm matters as much as a giant like Nvidia. That index was rising while he spoke, a sign to Lee that money was still in stocks.

By the close, it had slipped 0.79%. The regular S&P 500, where the biggest companies count most, fell 1.82%.

Bad Earnings Hit Tech the Same Day

Intel fell 28.6% after a weak fourth-quarter forecast, its worst day since 1974. Amazon reported $42.4 billion in negative free cash flow, driven by heavy AI spending.

A week earlier, Lee said yields back below 5% meant the AI selloff was ending. On Friday, the 10-year Treasury yield closed at 4.93%. The Nasdaq still had its worst day since June 5.

Steve Sosnick, chief strategist at Interactive Brokers, said his retail clients had not fled. On Thursday, though, they piled into Alphabet.

Why Lee Says Wall Street Is Waiting for November 3

Lee says big investors lack the conviction to buy falling stocks before Tuesday's midterm elections. Until then, he warned, a small push could send prices sharply lower.

"I think people are marking their calendar until November 3rd," he added.

CNBC's anchor said markets expect Democrats to edge ahead in both chambers of Congress. Sosnick called that the prevailing theory.

CME FedWatch also puts the odds of a December rate hike at 72%.

Lee says the buyers will come back. Tuesday's vote will show whether they do.

AMD Just Dropped 11% in a Day as Intel's PC Warning Rattles Chips. Is It Time to Sell, or Load Up? ©DragonImages and Thx4Stock via Canva
Key Takeaways

AMD shares fell 10.9% Friday to $505 after Intel's weak PC outlook triggered a chip rout, leaving the stock 23% below its 52-week high.

Lisa Su expects data center revenue to more than double in 2027, and AMD's partnership with Meta covers 6 gigawatts of GPUs.

AMD trades at 45.1x forward earnings, and the MI450 ramp could dilute gross margin as memory content rises.

Tuesday's report needs to beat the $13.09 billion revenue consensus and guide the fourth quarter toward a steeper data center ramp.

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD:NASDAQ) had a strong six months. Friday took a big bite out of it.

The stock fell 10.9% to $505 after Intel (INTC:NASDAQ) warned of weak PC demand, putting Intel on course for its worst day ever and dragging chip stocks down with it. AMD is still up 42.4% over six months, but it now sits 23% below its 52-week high of $659.

The timing stings. AMD reports third-quarter results on Tuesday, November 3, and its biggest AI customer story keeps growing. On October 27, AMD and Meta Platforms (META:NASDAQ) advanced a partnership that already covers 6 gigawatts of AMD GPUs.

So did Intel's warning say much about AMD? A little, and less than the selloff suggests.

Why Intel's news hit AMD

AMD still has real PC exposure. Its client business brought in $3.1 billion in the second quarter, up 23%, or about 27% of revenue by my math.

The mix, however, has shifted hard toward servers:

Data center revenue rose 107% to $6.7 billion.

Data center made up 58% of revenue, up from 42% a year earlier.

Gaming fell 31% on lower semi-custom sales.

Total revenue rose 50% to a record $11.5 billion, and non-GAAP EPS of $1.66 beat the $1.62 estimate.

Friday's drop wiped out weeks of gains in one session…

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD): share price, $ per share, last 6 months (TIKR)

With a five-year beta of 2.45, AMD tends to swing harder than the chip group in both directions.

Helios must carry the next leg

Lisa Su said in the second-quarter release that AI is driving "a significant expansion in demand for compute across all of our markets." The guidance backs her up.

AMD guided third-quarter revenue to about $13 billion, plus or minus $300 million, implying 41% growth. Consensus sits at $13.09 billion of revenue and $1.95 of EPS, with data center revenue expected near $8.27 billion.

Production shipments of the MI450 and Helios rack platform began in September, with a bigger ramp due in the fourth quarter and the first half of 2027. Su now expects data center revenue to more than double in 2027, with server CPU revenue up more than 70%.
